first-computer-bug-1947.summary: In 1947 operators of Harvard's Mark II traced a fault to a moth in a relay and taped it into the log as the first actual case of a bug. They removed it and taped it into their log book with this note: “First actual case of bug being found.” Engineers had called defects bugs long before electronic computers; Thomas Edison used it in an 1878 letter. Hopper, later a U.S. Navy rear admiral, popularized her moth story, and that log page is remembered as computing's first literal bug, though that word came first.

houssay-pituitary-nobel-1947.summary: In 1947 Bernardo Alberto Houssay shared a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work done at Universidad de Buenos Aires's Instituto de Fisiología since 1924: removing anterior pituitary tissue from dogs made with diabetes by pancreatectomy relieved their diabetes, and pituitary extracts caused it. These experiments, published with Alfredo Biasotti from 1930, showed that a pituitary hormone opposed insulin and placed hormonal regulation of carbohydrate metabolism on an experimental footing. Houssay's institute trained a generation including Luis Leloir and Eduardo Braun-Menéndez. Dismissed from his chair in 1943 by a military government, he worked on at a privately funded institute until reinstatement in 1955.

microwave-oven-1947.summary: In 1947 Raytheon sold the first microwave oven after radar melted an engineer's chocolate bar; it cost $5,000 and weighed 340 kilograms. Percy Spencer, Raytheon's self-taught engineer from Maine, had noticed in 1945 that microwaves from an active radar set melted his pocketed candy bar; microwave ovens feed magnetron power into a closed metal box, where it makes polar molecules in food rotate and produce heat (dielectric heating), and Raytheon filed for a patent on his cooking process on October 8, 1945. Tappan sold a licensed home model in 1956, and Raytheon, which bought Amana in 1965, introduced countertop ovens in 1967.

pulqui-jet-1947.summary: On August 9, 1947 Argentina flew the Pulqui I prototype, the first jet designed and built in Argentina and in Latin America, with test pilot First Lieutenant Osvaldo Weiss at its controls. Designed in 1946 at Argentina's Instituto Aerotécnico by engineers led by Frenchman Émile Dewoitine, it carried a Rolls-Royce Derwent 5 turbojet with its air intake in its nose; ducting around its cockpit left so little fuselage room that fuel tanks went into its wings, cutting range. Only one was completed, its performance was judged unsatisfactory, and work shifted to the more advanced Pulqui II.

transistor-1947.summary: In 1947 Bell Labs demonstrated the transistor, a switch with no moving parts, the building block of every chip. John Bardeen, Brattain and William Shockley had built on wartime work to make ultra-pure germanium for radar diodes; two gold contacts pressed very close together onto germanium made it amplify, and in that trial it worked as a speech amplifier with power gain of 18. Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared 1956's Nobel Prize in Physics, and transistors went on to replace vacuum tube triodes.

tukey-bit-1947.summary: In 1947 John Tukey coined the word bit for a binary digit, information theory's unit of information since. Claude Shannon's 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" first used it in print, crediting Tukey. Tukey is also credited with first using "software" for computer programs, in his 1958 American Mathematical Monthly article, and is best known for the Cooley–Tukey algorithm for computing Fourier transforms, developed with James Cooley.

woomera-range-1947.summary: In 1947 Britain and Australia set up a rocket range at Woomera, the Western world's largest land test range. Britain was too densely populated to test safely, so it asked Australia for a sparsely peopled site offering long firing corridors. Under their Anglo-Australian Joint Project of 1946, Woomera in South Australia was declared a prohibited area in 1947, an RAF Dakota landed at its airfield on 19 June 1947, and its first trial ran that December. Missile testing began in 1949, and Australia's first satellite, WRESAT, went up from Woomera in 1967, making Australia the fourth nation to orbit a satellite from its own territory.

cable-television-origins-1948.summary: In 1948 towns with no reception put an antenna on a hill and ran cable to homes; cable television began as a fix for mountains. They put large antennas on hills and mountaintops and ran coaxial trunk lines from them, to which homes in the community below connected. Local cable networks had relayed broadcasts before, in London (Rediffusion) and Berlin in 1936, and Switzerland also began in 1948, but in the United States cable grew into a commercial business in the 1950s. By 1968, 6.4 percent of American households had cable service, rising to 62.4 percent in 1994.

He traced its ideas to Harvard Medical School meetings where physicians discussed method with mathematicians and engineers, and to his work with Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer.

donora-smog-1948.summary: In October 1948 smog from a zinc works killed 20 people in Donora, Pennsylvania; 50 more died of respiratory causes within a month, and one third to one half of its 14,000 people fell ill. It held hydrogen fluoride and sulfur dioxide from U.S. Steel's Donora Zinc Works and American Steel & Wire plant over Donora; mixed with fog they formed yellow smog that lasted until rain fell on Sunday, October 31, and plant operators began shutting down only that morning.

ghawar-oil-field-1948.summary: In 1948 Ghawar was found in Saudi Arabia, the largest oil field on Earth; it has produced more than half of Saudi oil since. Measuring about 280 by 30 kilometres (some 8,400 square kilometres), it is by far the world's largest conventional oil field and is owned and operated by Saudi Aramco, the state oil company. Roughly 60 to 65 percent of all Saudi oil produced between 1948 and 2000 came from Ghawar, and cumulative output passed 65 billion barrels by early 2010.

grey-walter-tortoises-1949.summary: In 1949 Grey Walter built Elmer and Elsie, robot tortoises that sought light and avoided obstacles with two brain cells' worth of circuitry. He wanted to show that rich connections among a small number of brain cells could produce very complex behavior, that is, that how a brain worked lay in how it was wired. Three-wheeled and slow, hence nicknamed tortoises, they steered toward light (phototaxis) and could find their way to a recharging station when batteries ran low.

homeostat-1948.summary: In March 1948 Ross Ashby finished the Homeostat, four bomb-control units that adjusted to any disturbance and kept their own balance. It consisted of four interconnected Royal Air Force bomb control units with magnetically driven, water-filled potentiometers; each unit carried a magnet on top, and when any magnet was pushed off center it automatically changed its own configuration until all four returned to their central position, demonstrating what Ashby called ultrastability and illustrating his law of requisite variety. Ashby first described it in “Design for a Brain” in Electronic Engineering in December 1948.

lp-record-1948.summary: In June 1948 Columbia unveiled the LP, 20 minutes a side of vinyl; a symphony no longer needed six brittle discs. Records then were mostly abrasive, noisy shellac discs that played at about 78 rpm and held under five minutes per side; CBS Laboratories research chief Peter Goldmark led Columbia's team toward a disc holding at least 20 minutes per side, in research that began in 1939, paused for World War II and resumed in 1945. Their answer was a fine-grooved “microgroove” vinyl disc turning at 33⅓ rpm; Columbia's first release ran to 133 recordings, 85 of them 12-inch classical albums.

manchester-baby-1948.summary: In June 1948 Manchester's Baby ran a program held in its own memory, the first stored-program computer. Frederic C. Williams, Kilburn and Geoff Tootill built it to test Williams tubes, cathode-ray tube memories that gave truly random access: program and data sat in a single memory of 32 words of 32 bits, and hardware handled only subtraction and negation, leaving other arithmetic to software. Success led directly to their Manchester Mark 1, operational by April 1949, and then to Ferranti's Mark 1, the first commercially available general-purpose computer.

polaroid-instant-camera-1948.summary: In 1948 Edwin Land's Model 95 went on sale, the first camera to hand over a finished print a minute after its shutter clicked. His Model 95 Land Camera, introduced in 1948, a year after he unveiled instant film in New York City, is often called history's first commercial instant camera. It used roll film loaded as two rolls, one holding its negative and another its positive and developing agent, so that pictures developed inside the camera rather than in darkrooms. Polaroid filed for bankruptcy in February 2008 and stopped making instant film, but the Impossible Project took over one of its factories that year and revived film for its cameras.

toyota-production-system-1948.summary: From 1948 Toyota built cars only as orders came in and let any worker stop the line; lean production spread to every industry. Originally called just-in-time production, an idea from Toyota founder Kiichiro Toyoda, it drew its model from American supermarkets: each work center withdraws only parts it needs from a storage “shelf”, and whichever center makes those parts restocks just enough to replace them, which avoids overproduction. Its aims are to design out overburden (muri) and inconsistency (mura) and to eliminate waste (muda).

Detroit's Big Three had launched no new models since 1941 because of war production, which opened room for small automakers. Tucker Corporation ceased operations on March 3, 1949, amid negative press, an SEC investigation and a stock fraud trial; Tucker was acquitted of all charges in January 1950.

csirac-1949.summary: In November 1949 CSIRAC ran its first program in Sydney, Australia's first computer; in 1951 it was first to play music. Built in Sydney at CSIR's Radiophysics Laboratory by a team under Trevor Pearcey and Maston Beard, working largely independently of efforts in Europe and America, it was the fifth stored-program computer anywhere, used mercury acoustic delay lines holding 768 20-bit words as main memory and contained about 2,000 valves. In 1950 it was used to play music, the first known use of a digital computer for that purpose. Shut down for good in 1964, it survives as the oldest intact first-generation electronic computer.

fairness-doctrine-1949.summary: In 1949 the FCC required broadcasters that aired controversial public issues to present contrasting views; this rule shaped American news until its repeal in 1987. Its Editorializing Report repealed 1941's Mayflower doctrine, which had required stations to stay neutral in news and politics and barred editorial support for candidates, and instead obliged broadcast licensees to cover controversial issues of importance to their communities fairly and to air contrasting views on issues they addressed, offering airtime if a side was omitted. Stations had wide latitude, through news segments, public affairs shows or editorials, and equal time was not required, only contrasting views. On August 4, 1987, the FCC abolished it by a 4 to 0 vote.

It is often summarized as "Neurons that fire together, wire together," though Hebb stressed that cell A must help fire cell B, which requires A to fire just before B, foreshadowing spike-timing-dependent plasticity; groups of such co-active neurons form cell assemblies that could store memories. Artificial neural networks adopted his rule for adjusting weights.

In 1997 Mitchell Energy applied slickwater fracturing in north Texas's Barnett Shale, where a 1998 well's output made shale gas widely economical.

Written right to left with seven vowels, nineteen consonants and tone marks, N'ko (meaning 'I say') let Maninka, Bamana and Dyula speakers write their languages without Arabic or Latin letters. Kanté then wrote dictionaries, histories, translations of the Qur'an and medical texts in it. N'ko became a vehicle for indigenist historiography and a grassroots literacy movement that grew outside Sékou Touré's state language programme and spread through West Africa and its diaspora.

ratio-club-1949.summary: In 1949 John Bates founded the Ratio Club, a dining club of young British scientists who met for nine years to talk cybernetics. Built by Walter Zinn’s Argonne team in Idaho, it proved Enrico Fermi’s principle that a reactor can make more fuel than it consumes. groundnut-scheme-abandoned-1951.summary: A 1951 white paper (Cmd 8125) ended commercial groundnut production in Tanganyika, three years after Britain's Overseas Food Corporation set out to clear 3,210,000 acres with converted Sherman tanks and heavy tractors. Kongwa's soils baked hard, rainfall fell short, machinery broke on tree roots and groundnuts came in far below plan. About £36 million of public money was spent, and after 1951 Kongwa, Urambo and Nachingwea ran only as pilot and settlement schemes. Debates in both Houses of Parliament treated it as a lesson in planning from London without soil surveys or trials, and it became a standard reference in later arguments over large-scale agricultural projects across Africa.

Groundnuts were meant to ease Britain's post-war fats ration, and United Africa Company ran early clearing before Overseas Food Corporation took over in 1948. Lords debate in March 1951 argued over whether remaining acreage should pass to a Colonial Development Corporation or stay under a reconstituted body.

hela-cells-1951.summary: In 1951 cells taken from Henrietta Lacks without consent became HeLa, the first immortal human cell line, used for polio vaccines. George Otto Gey’s laboratory cultured them into HeLa, the first human cell line to live on in laboratory culture, dividing without limit. Gey gave them freely to other scientists, and HeLa has since served research on cancer, AIDS, radiation and gene mapping.

syntex-norethindrone-mexico-city-1951.summary: On 15 October 1951 Luis Ernesto Miramontes, a 26-year-old chemistry student from UNAM working at Syntex in Mexico City under George Rosenkranz and Carl Djerassi, completed a synthesis of 19-nor-17alpha-ethynyltestosterone, later named norethindrone. Syntex had been built on diosgenin from Mexican barbasco yams, which Russell Marker had shown could be converted to progesterone, and its chemists were racing to make steroids cheaper than European firms. Norethindrone was a progestin active when swallowed, far stronger than natural progesterone, and became an ingredient of early oral contraceptives from 1962. Gabriela Soto Laveaga's history follows barbasco trade from Oaxaca and Veracruz peasants who dug roots to Syntex's laboratories.

Their South Bank concerts on 26 July 1951 and BBC broadcasts gave outsiders a first hearing of a percussion instrument invented in Port of Spain in 1939 to 1946. Steelband went on to orchestral arrangements, Panorama competitions from 1963 and national-instrument status, while pan tuning remained a craft passed between workshops.

zybach-center-pivot-irrigation-1952.summary: Frank Zybach, tenant wheat farmer near Strasburg, Colorado, files on 27 June 1949 and on 22 July 1952 receives US Patent 2,604,359 for a self-propelled sprinkling irrigating apparatus: pipe on wheeled towers rotating around a central well, each driven by water pressure. With backer A. E. Trowbridge he builds systems in a rented Columbus, Nebraska shop, then in September 1954 sells exclusive manufacturing rights to Robert Daugherty's Valley Manufacturing of Valley, Nebraska, for a 5 percent royalty until patent expiry in 1969. Valley replaces water drive with electric motors and sells thousands across Ogallala Aquifer country. William Splinter's 1976 Scientific American article explains how pivots irrigate circles within 160-acre quarter sections with little labor on sandy, uneven land. Green circles now cover Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Egypt's desert.

karakum-canal-1954.summary: Construction starts in 1954 at Bosaga on the Amu Darya, cutting an unlined channel westward along desert margins. aedes-aegypti-eradication-americas-1958.summary: In 1947 Pan American Sanitary Organization member states adopted a Brazilian proposal to eradicate Aedes aegypti, vector of yellow fever and dengue, from every country in both Americas. vanguard-1-solar-satellite-1958.summary: In March 1958 Vanguard 1 became the first satellite powered by solar cells; it is still in orbit, humanity's oldest object in space. Though its signals stopped in 1964, it remains humanity's oldest artificial object in orbit, alongside its launch vehicle’s upper stage.

wairakei-geothermal-power-1958.summary: In November 1958 Wairakei geothermal power station near Taupo sent its first electricity into New Zealand's grid. Unlike Italy's Larderello, which used dry steam, Wairakei drew hot water and steam mixtures from wells up to 1,200 metres deep in Taupo Volcanic Zone, separating steam at wellhead through cyclone separators and flashing hot water at lower pressure, a design later copied worldwide. By March 1960, 69 megawatts had been commissioned and 192 megawatts were planned. Drilling began in 1950 during a post-war electricity shortage and a scheme to make heavy water that was later dropped.

Withdrawal of fluid caused ground subsidence of up to 15 metres in places and dried Geyser Valley, lessons that shaped later reinjection practice. Wairakei still operates, now with reinjection and a binary plant. New Zealand draws roughly a fifth of its electricity from geothermal fields, many on Maori-owned land under partnership arrangements.

zeta-fusion-claim-1958.summary: In 1958 Britain announced its ZETA machine had achieved fusion and retracted it within months; its neutrons were not from fusion. Leaked to journalists, that result was reported worldwide as outdoing Sputnik. On 16 May 1958 John Cockcroft published a retraction: measurements by Basil Rose had shown ZETA’s neutrons were directional and reversed with the current, indicating electrical rather than thermonuclear origin.

bacon-fuel-cell-1959.summary: In 1959 Tom Bacon demonstrated a hydrogen fuel cell that powered a welding rig and a forklift; its design flew to the Moon on Apollo. Bacon had developed his first practical hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell at Cambridge in 1932, reviving William Grove’s 1839 invention after a century of neglect; Pratt and Whitney licensed his patents in their successful bid to supply electrical power for Apollo.

Organized as CODASYL and drawing on Grace Hopper’s FLOW-MATIC, their committees approved specifications on 8 January 1960, printed as COBOL 60; meant as a stopgap, COBOL spread widely once Defense Department officials pressed manufacturers to supply it.

doordarshan-experimental-telecast-1959.summary: On 15 September 1959 President Rajendra Prasad inaugurates an experimental television service run by All India Radio from a Delhi studio, with UNESCO support and community receivers placed in teleclubs. Programmes go out for an hour twice a week to viewers within range of a small transmitter. Regular daily service follows in 1965; Bombay and Amritsar get stations in 1972; Doordarshan separates from All India Radio on 1 April 1976 as a department of its own; colour arrives with national programming on 15 August 1982. Rajagopal traces how this state broadcaster grew from a development tool for teleclubs into a national medium whose serials in 1987 drew mass audiences.

edsel-discontinued-1959.summary: On November 19, 1959 Ford announced its Edsel program's end after two years; accounts of its loss range from over $250 million to $350 million, and Edsel became a synonym for a flop. A recession had cut sales of all medium-priced cars, and buyers turned to economy models; sales from September 1957 to November 1959 came to about 116,000, less than half its projected break-even, and only 118,287 Edsels were built. Its plant capacity and tooling went into the compact Falcon, which sold over 400,000 in its first year.

groningen-gas-field-1959.summary: In 1959 drillers found Groningen's gas field under Dutch farmland, Europe's largest; the Dutch got rich and gave Dutch disease its name. Little noticed at first, Groningen proved Europe’s largest gas field, with some 2,740 billion cubic metres recoverable; nearly all of that country was connected to its gas, and its revenue helped build the Dutch welfare state.

It forms Lake Kariba, 280 kilometres long; Operation Noah removed animals threatened by rising waters from 1958 to 1961.

kdml105-jasmine-rice-1959.summary: In 1945 a district officer in Bang Khla, Chonburi, collects 199 panicles of a fragrant local rice, Khao Dawk Mali, from a farmer's field. Breeders at Khok Samrong rice station grow out pure lines, and after a decade of trials line 105 is released nationally in 1959 as Khao Dawk Mali 105. Its soft texture, pandan-like aroma and tall photoperiod-sensitive plant suit rainfed paddies of northeast Thailand. KDML105 and its mutant RD15 came to occupy around 4.3 million hectares, roughly a third of Thai rice land, yielding 9.4 million tonnes and anchoring Thailand's premium export trade under a protected Thai Hom Mali label.

kiwifruit-hayward-export-1959.summary: Seeds of Actinidia deliciosa reached New Zealand from Yichang, China in 1904 via Isabel Fraser and nurseryman Alexander Allison. Hayward Wright selected a large, long-keeping cultivar around 1924, and Te Puke orchards in Bay of Plenty began commercial planting in 1930s. Exports to Britain started in 1952, but US importers found 'Chinese gooseberry' unattractive during Cold War. In June 1959 Auckland exporter Turners and Growers adopted name 'kiwifruit' for a shipment to San Francisco. Hayward became near-universal cultivar worldwide, and by 1980s New Zealand's kiwifruit industry earned hundreds of millions of dollars yearly before Italy and later China overtook it in volume.

samuel-checkers-1959.summary: In 1959 Arthur Samuel's checkers program learned from its own games until it beat its author; he named the method machine learning. Written for IBM's first commercial computer, its 701, it scored positions and searched with alpha-beta pruning; its demonstration lifted IBM's stock 15 points overnight.

st-lawrence-seaway-1959.summary: In April 1959 St Lawrence Seaway opened: its rivers, locks, canals and channels let ocean ships sail from Atlantic waters through the Great Lakes to Duluth, Minnesota. Queen Elizabeth II, Prime Minister John Diefenbaker and President Dwight D. Eisenhower formally opened it on June 26, 1959.
